title: RBI Clubs 25 Card Payment Circulars Into A Single Framework
summary: RBI consolidates 25 card payment circulars into a single framework
detailed: Called the Reserve Bank of India (Digital Payments – Card-based transaction) Directions, 2026, the new norms look to streamline compliance and security rules for card-based digital payments.
The new guidelines consolidate all existing circulars related to card security, authentication, tokenisation, storage of card details and merchant discount rates (MDR).
The RBI’s new framework also directed credit card issuers to avoid restrictive network agreements and offer network choice at issuance or renewal.
Further, entities, other than card issuers and networks, are barred from storing actual card data for card-not-present payments.
sentences: Called the Reserve Bank of India (Digital Payments – Card-based transaction) Directions, 2026, the new norms look to streamline compliance and security rules for card-based digital payments.
The new rules also replace the need for referring multiple instructions issued over the years.

The new framework, which comes into force with immediate effect, primarily pertains to banks, non-bank payment system providers, and ecosystem participants under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act.
For end users, the notification does not add any new compliance, but instead brings all existing rules under one document.
The new guidelines consolidate all existing circulars related to card security, authentication, tokenisation, storage of card details and merchant discount rates (MDR).
The new framework retains the EMV chip standard for all cards.
It also noted that all point-of-sale (PoS) terminals and ATMs will continue to be EMV-compliant.
The new norms also incorporate the existing exemption (from additional authentication) for eligible contactless transactions of up to ₹5,000.
Domestic card transactions must settle in Indian currency via an Indian bank, reiterated the new guidelines.
The RBI’s new framework also directed credit card issuers to avoid restrictive network agreements and offer network choice at issuance or renewal.
However, issuers, which have disbursed 10 Lakh active cards or fewer, will be exempt from offering this choice.
Further, the rules also envisage new security and customer control mandates.
The central bank’s new rules also put the onus on regulated entities to ensure that card users have 24/7 controls to modify their transaction limits or to turn off their transactions altogether.
The framework also covers device, merchant-interface, and card-on-file (CoF) tokenisation.
Token service providers (TSPs) must gather explicit authenticated consent and not charge fees to cardholders, added the new norms.
The framework also notes that TSPs must also arrange system and security audits at least annually through CERT-In-empanelled auditors and file monthly reports.
Further, entities, other than card issuers and networks, are barred from storing actual card data for card-not-present payments.
The new rules also incorporate existing MDR ceilings for debit card transactions.
For small merchants with annual turnover of up to ₹20 Lakh, MDR remains capped at 0.4% for physical PoS payments, including online card transactions.
The rate for QR-based payment infrastructure has been set at 0.3% for small merchants.
For merchants with turnover above ₹20 Lakh, the MDR ceilings for PoS transactions and QR-based payments have been set at 0.9% and 0.8%, respectively.
The new rules also lay out customer protection mandates and grievance redressal mechanisms for the general public.
